claim: Tauopathies have diverse presentation, progression, and neuropathology.
source: Tauopathies have diverse presentation, progression, and neuropathology.
evidence: This is a general statement about tauopathies that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Tauopathies are linked to tau prion strains, self-replicating assemblies of unique quaternary conformation.
source: They are linked to tau prion strains, self-replicating assemblies of unique quaternary conformation, whose origin is unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by the authors' previous work and the experimental results presented in this manuscript.

claim: The origin of tau prion strains is unknown.
source: They are linked to tau prion strains, self-replicating assemblies of unique quaternary conformation, whose origin is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Tau strains can be propagated indefinitely in cultured cells.
source: Strains can be propagated indefinitely in cultured cells, and induce unique patterns of transmissible neuropathology upon inoculation into mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the authors' previous work and the current manuscript.

claim: Tau strains induce unique patterns of transmissible neuropathology upon inoculation into mice.
source: Strains can be propagated indefinitely in cultured cells, and induce unique patterns of transmissible neuropathology upon inoculation into mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mouse inoculation experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: DS9 and DS10 cell lines propagate different synthetic strains that derive from recombinant tau.
source: DS9 and DS10 cell lines propagate different synthetic strains that derive from recombinant tau.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Tau monomer adopts two conformational states: one that is inert (Mi) and one that is seed-competent (Ms).
source: We previously observed that tau monomer adopts two conformational states: one that is inert (Mi) and one that is seed-competent (Ms) (Mirbaha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Ms itself is comprised of multiple stable ensembles that encode unique strains.
source: We have now found that Ms itself is comprised of multiple stable ensembles that encode unique strains.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data throughout.

claim: DS9 monomer inoculated into naive cells encoded only DS9.
source: DS9 monomer inoculated into naive cells encoded only DS9, whereas DS10 monomer encoded multiple sub-strains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: DS10 monomer encoded multiple sub-strains.
source: DS9 monomer inoculated into naive cells encoded only DS9, whereas DS10 monomer encoded multiple sub-strains.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Tables 2-3.

claim: DS10 sub-strains each induced distinct pathology upon inoculation into a tauopathy mouse model (PS19).
source: Sub-strains each induced distinct pathology upon inoculation into a tauopathy mouse model (PS19).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: Ms purified from an Alzheimer's disease brain encoded a single strain.
source: Ms purified from an Alzeimer's disease brain encoded a single strain.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Ms from a corticobasal degeneration brain encoded three sub-strains.
source: Conversely, Ms from a corticobasal degeneration brain encoded three sub-strains, in which monomer from any one re-established all three upon inoculation into cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Tables 6-7.

claim: Monomer from any one CBD sub-strain re-established all three sub-strains upon inoculation into cells.
source: Conversely, Ms from a corticobasal degeneration brain encoded three sub-strains, in which monomer from any one re-established all three upon inoculation into cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 7.

claim: Seed competent tau monomer adopts multiple, stable seed-competent conformations, each of which encodes a limited number of strains.
source: Seed competent tau monomer thus adopts multiple, stable seed-competent conformations, each of which encodes a limited number of strains.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by all experimental data.

claim: Tauopathies include Alzheimer's disease (AD) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD), among many clinical and neuropathological syndromes.
source: They include Alzheimer's disease (AD) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD), among many clinical and neuropathological syndromes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tauopathies.

claim: Most tauopathies are sporadic.
source: Most are sporadic, and some are caused by dominant mutations in the microtubule associated protein tau (MAPT) gene (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Some tauopathies are caused by dominant mutations in the microtubule associated protein tau (MAPT) gene.
source: Most are sporadic, and some are caused by dominant mutations in the microtubule associated protein tau (MAPT) gene (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The origin of different sporadic tauopathies is poorly understood.
source: The origin of different sporadic tauopathies is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A single tau monomer stably propagates different structures in vitro, depending on the template to which it is initially exposed.
source: We initially hypothesized that they might arise from distinct, self-propagating assemblies based on our observation that a single tau monomer stably propagates different structures in vitro, depending on the template to which it is initially exposed (Frost et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Tau transmits amyloid pathology into cultured cells and mouse brain that can move from cell to cell.
source: Experiments from our group and others subsequently indicated that tau transmits amyloid pathology into cultured cells and mouse brain that can move from cell to cell (Frost et al., 2009b; Clavaguera et al., 2009), and led to the idea that it is 'prion-like.'
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tau is 'prion-like.'
source: Experiments from our group and others subsequently indicated that tau transmits amyloid pathology into cultured cells and mouse brain that can move from cell to cell (Frost et al., 2009b; Clavaguera et al., 2009), and led to the idea that it is 'prion-like.'
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations cited.

claim: Prion protein (PrP) prions form 'strains,' which are distinct amyloid structures derived from a single protein that propagate indefinitely in living systems.
source: Prion protein (PrP) prions form 'strains,' which are distinct amyloid structures derived from a single protein that propagate indefinitely in living systems, and which underlie diverse and predictable patterns of neuropathology in humans and mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about prion protein.

claim: PrP prion strains underlie diverse and predictable patterns of neuropathology in humans and mice.
source: Prion protein (PrP) prions form 'strains,' which are distinct amyloid structures derived from a single protein that propagate indefinitely in living systems, and which underlie diverse and predictable patterns of neuropathology in humans and mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about prion protein.

claim: Tau forms strains that can be isolated and propagated from cell to cell in a stable line that expresses the repeat domain (RD) containing two disease-associated mutations (P301L/V337M) fused to yellow fluorescent protein (RD-YFP).
source: We found that tau forms strains that can be isolated and propagated from cell to cell in a stable line that expresses the repeat domain (RD) containing two disease-associated mutations (P301L/V337M) fused to yellow fluorescent protein (RD-YFP).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work and experimental data.

claim: DS9 and DS10 are two 'artificial' strains based on inoculation of recombinant fibrils into RD-YFP cells and isolation of two clonal lines that stably propagated aggregates of distinct conformation.
source: We initially created two 'artificial' strains based on inoculation of recombinant fibrils into RD-YFP cells and isolation of two clonal lines that stably propagated aggregates of distinct conformation: DS9 and DS10.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work and experimental data.

claim: Inoculation of DS9 and DS10 lysates into PS19 mice created distinct neuropathological phenotypes.
source: Inoculation of DS9 and DS10 lysates into a mouse model of tauopathy (PS19) that is based on expression of 1N4R human tau with a single disease-associated mutation (P301S) (Yoshiyama et al., 2007), created distinct neuropathological phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PS19 is a mouse model of tauopathy based on expression of 1N4R human tau with a single disease-associated mutation (P301S).
source: Inoculation of DS9 and DS10 lysates into a mouse model of tauopathy (PS19) that is based on expression of 1N4R human tau with a single disease-associated mutation (P301S) (Yoshiyama et al., 2007), created distinct neuropathological phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the literature describing the PS19 mouse model.

claim: DS9 and DS10 neuropathological phenotypes could be transmitted stably across multiple generations of mice.
source: These could be transmitted stably across multiple generations of mice, and finally back into the RD-YFP biosensor cells, where DS9 and DS10 strains displayed their original morphology (Sanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DS9 and DS10 strains displayed their original morphology when transmitted back into RD-YFP biosensor cells.
source: These could be transmitted stably across multiple generations of mice, and finally back into the RD-YFP biosensor cells, where DS9 and DS10 strains displayed their original morphology (Sanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Distinct tau strain ensembles were isolated from the brains of patients with different tauopathies using RD-YFP biosensor cells.
source: Additionally, using the RD-YFP biosensor cells we isolated distinct tau strain ensembles from the brains of patients with different tauopathies.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work.

claim: Different tau strains are linked to various neuropathological syndromes.
source: This linked different strains to the various neuropathological syndromes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' previous work.

claim: Tau is not known to cause infectious neurodegenerative disease in humans.
source: Unlike the prion protein (PrP), tau is not known to cause infectious neurodegenerative disease in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tau.

claim: Tau should be considered a prion.
source: However, after creating two classes of infectious proteinaceous particles from recombinant protein that accounted for distinct and stably transmissible patterns of neuropathology, we proposed that tau should be considered a prion (Sanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposal based on experimental observations cited.

claim: 18 distinct tau prion strains were created that following intracerebral inoculation in mice created distinct pathological patterns and rates of progression.
source: Subsequently, we created 18 distinct tau prion strains and observed that following intracerebral inoculation in mice they created distinct pathological patterns and rates of progression (Kaufman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Others had previously made similar observations of neuropathological diversity upon inoculation of tau fibril preparations from human tauopathies.
source: Indeed, others had previously made similar observations of neuropathological diversity upon inoculation of tau fibril preparations from human tauopathies (Clavaguera et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by others.

claim: The diversity of tauopathy can be explained in large part by the strains that underlie them, in other words, by protein conformation.
source: We have concluded that, in addition to probable contributions of environmental and genetic factors, the diversity of tauopathy can be explained in large part by the strains that underlie them, in other words, by protein conformation (Kaufman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the authors' previous work.

claim: Mi does not spontaneously self-assemble or seed aggregation.
source: Although Mi does not spontaneously self-assemble or seed aggregation, Ms has a distinct conformation that allows self-assembly and seeding activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Ms has a distinct conformation that allows self-assembly and seeding activity.
source: Although Mi does not spontaneously self-assemble or seed aggregation, Ms has a distinct conformation that allows self-assembly and seeding activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Ms has been isolated from recombinant sources and human brain.
source: We have isolated Ms from recombinant sources and human brain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Ms retains its activity following isolation by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and passage through a 100kD cutoff filter.
source: It retains its activity following isolation by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and passage through a 100kD cutoff filter (Mirbaha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Ms is differentiated from Mi based on exposure of critical amino acids (275VQIINK280/306VQIVYK311) that mediate amyloid formation.
source: Structural studies (Mirbaha et al., 2018) suggest that Ms is differentiated from Mi based on exposure of critical amino acids (275VQIINK280/306VQIVYK311) that have previously been determined to mediate amyloid formation (von Bergen et al., 2000; von Bergen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Mi, critical amino acids 275VQIINK280/306VQIVYK311 are predicted to be buried in hairpins and rendered relatively inaccessible for intermolecular interactions.
source: In Mi they are predicted to be buried in hairpins and rendered relatively inaccessible for intermolecular interactions.
evidence: This is a prediction based on structural studies cited.

claim: 52 clones derived from DS9 monomer isolated by SEC exhibited the speckled conformation previously observed for DS9.
source: For Ms derived from DS9, we observed no variation—each of 52 clones exhibited the speckled conformation previously observed for DS9 (Sanders et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: 31 monoclonal lines derived from DS9 lysate passed through a 100 kD size exclusion filter were indistinguishable from DS9 by confocal microscopy.
source: In addition, we passed the lysate through a 100 kD size exclusion filter and used it to inoculate DS1 cells, creating 31 monoclonal lines. All were indistinguishable from DS9 by confocal microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Inoculation using unfractionated DS9 lysate, or lysate of any of the sub-strains produced a single population of clones, all identical to DS9 in morphology.
source: Inoculation using unfractionated DS9 lysate, or lysate of any of the sub-strains produced a single population of clones, all identical to DS9 in morphology (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DS9 and DS9.1–9.6 exhibited similar limited proteolysis patterns, with bands at 10 kD, and between 20 and 25 kD.
source: DS9 and DS9.1–9.6 exhibited very similar limited proteolysis patterns, with bands at 10 kD, and between 20 and 25 kD (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DS1 had no protease resistant species.
source: DS1 had no protease resistant species.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DS9 and DS9.1–9.6 exhibited similar fractionation patterns, with most tau being insoluble.
source: DS9 and DS9.1–9.6 exhibited similar fractionation patterns, with most tau being insoluble (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DS9 and DS9.1–9.6 had identical maximal seeding, with variation in the dose responses within ~1 log of concentration.
source: DS9 and DS9.1–9.6 had identical maximal seeding, with variation in the dose responses within ~1 log of concentration, which is typical for independent isolates of the same strain (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inoculation with unfractionated DS10 lysate produced a single population of clones, all identical to DS10.
source: As we have previously reported, inoculation with unfractionated DS10 lysate produced a single population of clones, all identical to DS10 (Sanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DS10 monomer created five distinct sub-strains, easily discerned by inclusion morphology.
source: However, DS10 monomer created five distinct sub-strains, easily discerned by inclusion morphology: 36% were ordered (and indistinguishable from the parent strain) termed DS10.1; 21% were speckled, termed DS10.2; 13% were thread-like, termed DS10.3; 9% were disorganized, termed DS10.4 (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Table 2.

claim: 36% of DS10 monomer-derived clones were ordered and indistinguishable from the parent strain, termed DS10.1.
source: However, DS10 monomer created five distinct sub-strains, easily discerned by inclusion morphology: 36% were ordered (and indistinguishable from the parent strain) termed DS10.1; 21% were speckled, termed DS10.2; 13% were thread-like, termed DS10.3; 9% were disorganized, termed DS10.4 (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: 21% of DS10 monomer-derived clones were speckled, termed DS10.2.
source: However, DS10 monomer created five distinct sub-strains, easily discerned by inclusion morphology: 36% were ordered (and indistinguishable from the parent strain) termed DS10.1; 21% were speckled, termed DS10.2; 13% were thread-like, termed DS10.3; 9% were disorganized, termed DS10.4 (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: 13% of DS10 monomer-derived clones were thread-like, termed DS10.3.
source: However, DS10 monomer created five distinct sub-strains, easily discerned by inclusion morphology: 36% were ordered (and indistinguishable from the parent strain) termed DS10.1; 21% were speckled, termed DS10.2; 13% were thread-like, termed DS10.3; 9% were disorganized, termed DS10.4 (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: 9% of DS10 monomer-derived clones were disorganized, termed DS10.4.
source: However, DS10 monomer created five distinct sub-strains, easily discerned by inclusion morphology: 36% were ordered (and indistinguishable from the parent strain) termed DS10.1; 21% were speckled, termed DS10.2; 13% were thread-like, termed DS10.3; 9% were disorganized, termed DS10.4 (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: Approximately 21% of DS10 monomer-derived cells formed a fifth strain, DS10.5, that rapidly 'sectored,' that is, lost its inclusions, and thus could not be further characterized.
source: Approximately 21% of cells formed a fifth strain, DS10.5, that rapidly 'sectored,' that is, lost its inclusions, and thus could not be further characterized.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2.

claim: DS10 and DS10.1 exhibited similar protease resistant doublets around 10 kD and a relatively light band around 20 kD.
source: DS10 and DS10.1 exhibited similar protease resistant doublets around 10 kD and a relatively light band around 20 kD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DS10.2 exhibited bands at 10 kD and between 20 and 25 kD.
source: DS10.2 exhibited bands at 10 kD and between 20 and 25 kD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DS10.3 and 10.4 exhibited a band at 15 kD.
source: DS10.3 and 10.4 exhibited a band at 15 kD.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DS10.3 exhibited a band at 10 kD, which was mostly absent in DS10.4.
source: DS10.3 exhibited a band at 10 kD, which was mostly absent in DS10.4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: DS10, DS10.1 and DS10.2 primarily contained an insoluble fraction and a small soluble fraction.
source: DS10, DS10.1 and DS10.2 primarily contained an insoluble fraction and a small soluble fraction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DS10.3 and DS10.4 exhibited mixed solubility, with about half soluble and insoluble tau.
source: By contrast, DS10.3 and DS10.4 exhibited mixed solubility, with about half soluble and insoluble tau (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DS10 sub-strains had very different seeding efficiency that spanned >2 log orders of concentration.
source: DS10 sub-strains also had very different seeding efficiency that spanned >2 log orders of concentration (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DS10 and DS10.1 had almost identical seeding profiles, with an EC50 of 300 ng for clarified lysate.
source: DS10 and DS10.1 had almost identical seeding profiles, with an EC50 of 300 ng for clarified lysate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DS10.2 had an EC50 of 10 ng.
source: DS10.2 had an EC50 of 10 ng.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DS10.3 had a much weaker seeding activity with an EC50 at >10 μg (unable to be determined accurately), and reduced maximal seeding efficiency at ~50%.
source: DS10.3 had a much weaker seeding activity with an EC50 at >10 μg (unable to be determined accurately), and reduced maximal seeding efficiency at ~50%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DS10.4 had an EC50 of 100 ng.
source: DS10.4 had an EC50 of 100 ng.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In 49 sub-strains derived from DS10.1 monomer, 45 appeared identical to DS10.1, except for four that formed DS10.5 (sectored).
source: In 49 sub-strains derived from DS10.1 monomer, 45 appeared identical to DS10.1, except for four that formed DS10.5 (sectored) (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: Ms from DS10.1 was relatively restricted in its conformation.
source: This suggested Ms from DS10.1 was relatively restricted in its conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: Ms derived from each of DS10.2, DS10.3, or DS10.4 gave rise to all sub-strains, including DS10.1, with predomination of the original sub-strain.
source: Ms derived from each of DS10.2, DS10.3, or DS10.4 gave rise to all sub-strains, including DS10.1, with predomination of the original sub-strain (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: Ms from DS10.2, DS10.3, and DS10.4 existed as conformational ensemble.
source: This indicated that Ms from these DS10 substrains existed as conformational ensemble.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: Multimeric assemblies from total lysate exhibit consistent strain behavior in all cases, that is, faithful replication.
source: Taken together, our experiments revealed that while multimeric assemblies from total lysate exhibit consistent strain behavior in all cases, that is, faithful replication, tau monomer (Ms) is less constrained.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tau monomer (Ms) is less constrained than multimeric assemblies.
source: Taken together, our experiments revealed that while multimeric assemblies from total lysate exhibit consistent strain behavior in all cases, that is, faithful replication, tau monomer (Ms) is less constrained.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ms derived from DS9 was completely restricted to forming a single strain.
source: While Ms derived from DS9 was completely restricted to forming a single strain, and Ms from DS10.1 predominantly encoded one sub-strain, others (DS10.2, DS10.3, DS10.4) adopted a defined set of strains in which Ms from any could give rise to all five.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Ms from DS10.1 predominantly encoded one sub-strain.
source: While Ms derived from DS9 was completely restricted to forming a single strain, and Ms from DS10.1 predominantly encoded one sub-strain, others (DS10.2, DS10.3, DS10.4) adopted a defined set of strains in which Ms from any could give rise to all five.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: Ms from DS10.2, DS10.3, and DS10.4 adopted a defined set of strains in which Ms from any could give rise to all five.
source: While Ms derived from DS9 was completely restricted to forming a single strain, and Ms from DS10.1 predominantly encoded one sub-strain, others (DS10.2, DS10.3, DS10.4) adopted a defined set of strains in which Ms from any could give rise to all five.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Table 3.

claim: Mice inoculated with DS1 controls exhibited no tau pathology in the hippocampus, CA1, or CA3.
source: Mice inoculated with DS1 controls exhibited no tau pathology in the hippocampus, CA1, or CA3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: DS9 and DS10, and all sub-strains induced different types of pathology.
source: DS9, DS10, and all sub-strains induced different types of pathology.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: DS9 and DS9.1 induced tangle-like inclusions throughout CA1 and CA3 in patterns that were indistinguishable from one another.
source: DS9 and DS9.1 induced tangle-like inclusions throughout CA1 and CA3 in patterns that were indistinguishable from one another, consistent with prior observations (Sanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: DS10 induced AT8-positive puncta in mossy fiber tracts of the hippocampus with strong staining patterns in the cell body, and AT8-positive puncta in CA3.
source: As expected, DS10 induced AT8-positive puncta in mossy fiber tracts of the hippocampus with strong staining patterns in the cell body, and AT8-positive puncta in CA3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: DS10.1 induced pathology similar to DS10 in both CA1 and CA3.
source: DS10.1 induced pathology similar to DS10 in both CA1 and CA3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: DS10.2 induced tangle-like inclusions throughout CA1, but with little or no pathology in CA3.
source: DS10.2 induced tangle-like inclusions throughout CA1, but with little or no pathology in CA3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: DS10.3 had very low seeding efficiency and induced pathology only in CA1.
source: DS10.3 had very low seeding efficiency and induced pathology only in CA1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: DS10.4 had low seeding and induced pathology only in CA1.
source: DS10.4 also had low seeding and induced pathology only in CA1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 4.

claim: DS9 and DS9.1 were indistinguishable by blinded analysis of AT8 signal in hippocampi of injected mice.
source: DS9 and DS9.1 were indistinguishable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 4.

claim: DS10.1–10.3 were all easily distinguished by blinded analysis, with a single error for DS10.4, which was misclassified in one instance.
source: DS10.1–10.3 were all easily distinguished, with a single error for DS10.4, which was misclassified in one instance (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 4.

claim: Strain composition in AD and CBD patient brains is quite distinct.
source: We have previously determined strain composition in AD and CBD patient brains to be quite distinct (Sanders et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Total lysate from an AD patient produced a single clonal morphology, AD(t).
source: We inoculated DS1 cells with total lysate from an AD patient and recovered a single clonal morphology, AD(t).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: AD Ms isolated by SEC produced an identical clonal morphology to AD(t), termed AD(m).
source: We also used AD Ms isolated by SEC to inoculate DS1 cells and recovered an identical clonal morphology, AD(m).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Each AD clone exhibited a single 'speckled' conformation, indicating that a single strain was most likely propagated.
source: As we had previously observed (Sanders et al., 2014), each clone exhibited a single 'speckled' conformation, indicating that we had most likely propagated a single strain (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 4A and citation to previous work.

claim: All AD clones derived from Ms isolated by passage through a 100 kD cutoff filter had similar morphological characteristics to AD(t) and AD(m).
source: We also isolated AD Ms by passage through a 100 kD cutoff filter and inoculated DS1 cells, isolating 23 monoclonal lines. All clones had similar morphological characteristics to AD(t) and AD(m) (Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 5.

claim: AD(t) and AD(m) clones revealed identical digestion patterns by limited proteolysis.
source: To better characterize the tau prions, we performed limited proteolysis on the lysates from AD(t) and AD(m) clones. This revealed identical digestion patterns (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Strains derived from AD(m) or AD(t) consisted of both soluble and insoluble protein.
source: Strains derived from AD(m) or AD(t) consisted of both soluble and insoluble protein (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Seeding analyses from the AD(t) and AD(m) cell lines revealed very similar potencies.
source: Seeding analyses from the cell lines also revealed very similar potencies (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tau Ms from the AD patient encoded the same single strain as total lysate.
source: We concluded that tau Ms from the AD patient encoded the same single strain as total lysate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Table 5.

claim: Total CBD lysate produced two distinct strains: CBD1(t) and CBD2(t).
source: Upon transduction of the DS1 cells, the total CBD lysate produced two distinct strains: CBD1(t) and CBD2(t).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Ms from the CBD brain created two strains identical to those derived from total lysate CBD1(m) and CBD2(m), plus a third strain, CBD3(m).
source: Ms from the CBD brain created two strains identical to those derived from total lysate CBD1(m) and CBD2(m), plus a third strain, CBD3(m) (Figure 5A, Table 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Table 6.

claim: Tau from clones CBD1(t) and CBD1(m), or CBD2(t) and CBD2(m) exhibited similar sedimentation properties.
source: Whether derived from total lysate or monomer, tau from clones CBD1(t) and CBD1(m), or CBD2(t) and CBD2(m) exhibited similar sedimentation properties (Figure 5B), proteolysis patterns (Figure 5C), and seeding activities (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Tau from clones CBD1(t) and CBD1(m), or CBD2(t) and CBD2(m) exhibited similar proteolysis patterns.
source: Whether derived from total lysate or monomer, tau from clones CBD1(t) and CBD1(m), or CBD2(t) and CBD2(m) exhibited similar sedimentation properties (Figure 5B), proteolysis patterns (Figure 5C), and seeding activities (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Tau from clones CBD1(t) and CBD1(m), or CBD2(t) and CBD2(m) exhibited similar seeding activities.
